findings: Ara naming, boundary/projection distinction, target binding, source count and 150–220-word length pass.
Westerlund 1 is explicitly placed in Ara by NASA. Dust/infrared wording and Westerlund 1-26 classification/radius accurately follow the opened sources.

The Dec-2025 Fermi claim is correctly time-bounded and qualified: the over-650-light-year bubble/nascent outflow is distinct from the 2022 H.E.S.S. ring; article does not collapse the hypotheses into fact.
Caelum name/abbreviation, projection distinction, target binding, self-check, source count and 150–220-word length pass.
LHS 1678 in Caelum was checked from primary Gaia coordinates in the original paper against the IAU Caelum boundary, rather than inferred from the system name.

The original study supports validated b/c and 0.86/3.69-day periods while d was still a candidate; the opened 2024 article supports validation of d and its roughly Earth-size radius. The revision narrative is accurate.

evidence.detail: IAU table confirms Ara/Ara/the Altar and Caelum/Cae/the Engraving Tool. Its significance section says original constellation patterns generally have no physical connection. The published Caelum boundary vertices were also opened.

NASA page dated/updated 18 Dec 2025 places Westerlund 1 in Ara; says Fermi data show a gamma-ray bubble over 650 light-years long below the Milky Way plane, calls it a nascent outflow likely recently produced by massive young cluster stars, and distinguishes the H.E.S.S. 2022 gamma-ray ring.
NASA/ESA Hubble identifies Westerlund 1-26 as a red supergiant, sometimes classed as a hypergiant, with radius over 1,500 Suns; source describes Westerlund 1 as a young super star cluster.
2024 article validates third planet d using TESS and new ground-based light curves; radius 0.98 ± 0.07 Earth radii and 4.97-day orbit.

Original primary paper directly opened as the underlying study mirrored by the listed CaltechAUTHORS record. It validates b/c by ground follow-up at 0.86/3.69 days and retains d as a 4.97-day candidate; primary PDF table gives Gaia DR2 position RA 68.1789866°, Dec −39.7908744°.

Using the primary-paper Gaia coordinate and IAU's opened Caelum boundary vertices, an independent point-in-polygon check places LHS 1678 within Caelum. Thus the article's direction claim is factually resolved rather than inferred from the name.

Direct open returned the web reader's Internal Error. The linked study's primary arXiv record/PDF was opened independently; this is an access limitation of the record endpoint, not a factual contradiction.
